clinician.trajectory_summary: A 21-year-old woman presented with 3 weeks of subjective visual impairment and blurry vision. Initial ophthalmic examination at two prior departments and on current admission revealed completely normal objective findings (6/6 visual acuity, normal fundus, normal OCT, normal visual fields), consistent with retrobulbar optic neuritis; she was initially misclassified as having psychosomatic disturbances. Six weeks after symptom onset (3 weeks after the normal eye exam), she developed acute lower limb weakness and clinical transverse myelitis. Spinal cord MRI demonstrated lesions extending over 3 vertebral segments (longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis). Brain MRI showed 3 lesions that did not meet diagnostic criteria for multiple sclerosis, while orbital MRI revealed no lesions. NMO-IgG serology returned positive, confirming Devic's syndrome. She was treated with IV steroids. At 4-year follow-up, visual function remained relatively preserved (6/9 both eyes), but she experienced significant residual disability from myelopathy with urinary incontinence and walking disorders.

key_supporting_evidence.claim: Initial presentation with subjective visual symptoms but normal objective ophthalmic examination (retrobulbar optic neuritis)
Development of acute transverse myelitis 6 weeks after initial visual symptoms
Spinal cord MRI demonstrating longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis (LETM) extending over 3 vertebral segments
Brain MRI showing lesions not meeting diagnostic criteria for multiple sclerosis
NMO-IgG seropositive status confirming the diagnosis
Long-term outcome at 4 years showing preserved vision but progressive myelopathic disability (urinary incontinence and walking disorders)

ruled_out_or_less_likely_alternatives.basis: Brain MRI lesions did not meet diagnostic criteria for MS, and the presence of LETM (3 vertebral segments) with NMO-IgG positivity favors Devic's syndrome over MS
Initial misclassification was contradicted by subsequent objective development of transverse myelitis, MRI-confirmed spinal cord lesions, and serological confirmation of organic autoimmune disease
Development of transverse myelitis and NMO-IgG positivity establishes this as part of the NMO spectrum rather than isolated optic neuritis
